text.en: You are a young traveller setting off across the subcontinent in the 7th century. The Guptas are gone, yet the land is busy and vibrant. You meet kings and poets, monks and merchants, temple builders and scholars. In this chapter we take a quick tour of the powers of the time, from Kannauj to Kanchipuram, and the life of the people.

Harshavardhana, or Harsha, ruled from Kannauj. He was also a fine poet and dramatist and is believed to be the author of three Sanskrit plays about love, courtly life and sacrifice. His court poet Bana wrote a masterpiece of classical Indian literature, a novel which he died before finishing and which was completed by his son. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang described Kannauj as a beautiful and prosperous city and Harsha as a just and energetic ruler with a vast army, often on military campaigns. Kannauj later became the centre of a long and inconclusive three-way fight among the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Palas and the Rashtrakutas, often called the Tripartite Struggle.
The Palas of Bengal and Bihar were great patrons of Mahayana Buddhism and founded major monasteries such as Vikramashila in Bihar and Somapura in present-day Bangladesh. At Nalanda nearly 3,000 scholars studied grammar, logic, Hindu and Buddhist philosophy, and rituals. The Gurjara-Pratiharas ruled much of north India. Their ruler Bhoja was known as Mihira, a name of the Sun, and Adi Varaha, a name for Vishnu as the boar. Kashmir stayed well connected to the rest of India despite its mountains. King Lalitaditya Muktapida defeated an Arab chief three times according to the Rajatarangini of Kalhana. In the late 10th century Queen Dida consolidated power through alliances and ruthlessly removed rivals. People often did not regard Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism as separate but as branches of a common philosophical tree.
The Rashtrakutas patronised Hindu, Buddhist and Jain thought and encouraged learning and literature in Sanskrit, Prakrit and Kannada. Their carved Durga panel shows a dynamic composition of the goddess's assault on a demon. Records of Arab travellers speak well of their tolerance and of mosques that were built for prayers. The Chalukyas of Badami: Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha and rival kingdoms, as the court poet Ravikirti recorded in a poetic inscription. When Harsha tried to go further south he retreated, keeping the Tungabhadra river as an unwritten boundary between the powers. The eastern branch later became independent. The Pallavas of Kanchipuram, allied with the Chalukyas, built great temples and sculpture at places such as Mahabalipuram. The Cholas rose again from their capital at Thanjavur and were to control much of south India in time. Many inscriptions were written in two languages, such as Sanskrit and a local tongue, so that rulers and the local people could both read them.
Directly governed lands were divided into provinces (bhuktis or rashtras), districts (mandalas) and villages, with officials at every level. Society remained largely rural and agrarian, and classical texts on farming reflect the emphasis on agriculture. Two major merchant guilds worked in south India: one in coastal and inland trade, and the other the largest inter-regional merchant association. Some terms such as asprishya, not to be touched, appeared in a few texts and point to discrimination against communities regarded as impure. Some dynasties also had female rulers, like Tribhuvana Mahadevi I of the Bhauma-Karas in Odisha in the 9th century.
Brahmagupta, born in 598 CE in Bhillamala, the first capital of the Gurjara-Pratiharas, did remarkable work in mathematics and astronomy. Royal patronage sustained a long tradition of art and learning. Jainism remained popular in western India and Karnataka with support from rulers and wealthy merchants. The Alvars and Nayanars, poet-saints of the south, sang devotion to Vishnu and Shiva. Arab traders and rulers reached Sindh. The Chachnama records the resistance of the queen of Raja Dahar after his death. The Huns, who had weakened the Gupta empire, could not affect India much at that time. This turbulent period was not a historical void. It saw the integration of new social and political groups, the growth of literature in Sanskrit and regional languages, and major advances in temple architecture and sculpture.

problem.en: Why did rulers write inscriptions in two languages?

text.en: One language, such as Sanskrit, was used for formal court records.
The other was the local language of the people.

why.en: So common people could read the message.

text.en: Thus a message reached both scholars and ordinary people.

prompt.en: Compare the Palas and the Rashtrakutas as patrons of learning.

requiredIdeas.en: Palas supported Mahayana Buddhism and monasteries.
Rashtrakutas supported many faiths and Kannada literature.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking this era was a dark age.

points.en: After the Guptas, Harsha, Palas, Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas, Chalukyas, Pallavas and Cholas shaped India.
Kannauj was the centre of the Tripartite Struggle.
Monasteries like Nalanda and Vikramashila were centres of learning.
Art, literature and temple architecture flourished.
